skills.name: Solve simultaneous linear equations by drawing graphs

note.text:
To solve two linear equations with graphs:
1. Make a table of values for each line (three points are enough; the third is a check).
2. Draw both lines on the same axes.
3. The point where they cross gives the solution: its x-coordinate and its y-coordinate.
Example: y = x + 1 and y = −x + 5 cross at (2, 3), so x = 2 and y = 3.
Check by substituting into both equations. Parallel lines (same gradient) never cross: no solution.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to draw two straight lines from tables of values and read the solution of the simultaneous equations from where they cross.
Builds on: Form Three straight-line graphs (y = mx + c) and Lesson {16}.
Leads to: Lessons {21} and {22} (regions), where lines become the edges of a solution set.

sections.heading: From equation to line
sections.text:
Each linear equation, such as y = x + {1}, has many solutions: ({0}, {1}), ({1}, {2}), ({2}, {3}) … On a graph they make a straight line.
To draw it, make a table with three values of x, work out y, plot the points and join them with a ruler. The third point is a check: if it is not in line, a value is wrong.
For y = −x + {5}: x = {0} gives {5}, x = {2} gives {3}, x = {4} gives {1}.

sections.heading: Reading the solution
sections.text:
Draw y = x + {1} and y = −x + {5} on the same axes. They cross at ({2}, {3}).
That point is on both lines, so it satisfies both equations: x = {2}, y = {3}.
Check: {2} + {1} = {3} and −{2} + {5} = {3}.
Read the x-coordinate first (across), then y (up). If the crossing is between grid lines, give the closest reading and check algebraically. Lines with the same gradient are parallel: no solution.

key_words.meaning: two equations that must both be true at once
chosen x values with the y values worked out
the steepness m in y = mx + c

examples: y = {mono(2, 'x')} and y = x + {3} cross at ({3}, {6})

mistake.why: Coordinates are written (x, y): across first, then up.

steps: Draw both lines. They cross at ({h}, {k}).
Check: {m1 * h + c1} = {k} and {m2 * h + c2} = {k}.

cards.idea: Each line is the picture of all the solutions of one equation.
example: Every point on y = x + {1} satisfies the equation: ({0}, {1}), ({1}, {2}), ({2}, {3}) …

cards.idea: The crossing point satisfies both equations at once: it is the solution.
Parallel lines never cross, so the equations have no solution.
example: y = {mono(2, 'x')} + {1} and y = {mono(2, 'x')} − {3}: same gradient, no crossing

check.prompt: How many solutions do y = {poly([m, 'x'], [c1, ''])} and y = {poly([m, 'x'], [c2, ''])} have?

distractors.text: Infinitely many: the lines are the same

misconceptions.explain: Lines with the same gradient never meet.
Two straight lines can cross at most once.
The lines cross the y-axis at {c1} and {c2}: different lines.

solution: Both lines have gradient {m}, so they are parallel.
The y-intercepts {c1} and {c2} are different, so they are not the same line.

questions.prompt: Complete the table of values for y = {poly([m, 'x'], [c, ''])}. What is y when x = {t}?
where: m * t + c != m + t + c

questions.prompt: The graph shows lines A and B. Use it to solve their two equations.

misconceptions.explain: Read x across (horizontal) first, then y up: the point is ({h}, {k}).
({0}, {c1}) is where line A meets the y-axis. Line B does not pass through it.
The crossing is at height y = {k}, not on the x-axis.

solution: The solution is where the lines cross.

questions.prompt: The lines y = {poly([m1, 'x'], [c1, ''])} and y = {poly([m2, 'x'], [c2, ''])} are drawn. At what value of x do they cross?

misconceptions.explain: {k} is the y-coordinate of the crossing. The question asks for x.
Divide by {m1 - m2}: x = {c2 - c1} ÷ {br(m1 - m2)} = {h}.

solution: At the crossing both y values are equal: {poly([m1, 'x'], [c1, ''])} = {poly([m2, 'x'], [c2, ''])}.
Check on the graph: at x = {h} both lines have y = {k}.

questions.prompt: Asong drew y = {poly([m1, 'x'], [c1, ''])} and y = {poly([m2, 'x'], [c2, ''])} and read off the crossing as ({h + 1}, {k}). Is that right?
questions.correct: No: x = {h + 1} gives y = {m1 * (h + 1) + c1} on the first line and {m2 * (h + 1) + c2} on the second. The lines cross at ({h}, {k})

distractors.text: Yes: the point is on both lines
No: the lines are parallel and never cross

misconceptions.explain: Substitute x = {h + 1}: y = {m1 * (h + 1) + c1} and y = {m2 * (h + 1) + c2} are different.
The gradients {m1} and {m2} are different, so the lines do cross.
({k}, {h}) has x and y swapped. Check: it does not satisfy y = {poly([m1, 'x'], [c1, ''])}.

solution: Substitute x = {h + 1}: the two lines give different y values, so it is not on both.
